turns.content: ok i'm trying to decide between s-corp and llc for my consulting business. revenue is like 180k a year. what's smarter

Good question to be sitting with. At $180k, the S-corp election often starts making real sense — the core play is splitting income between salary and distributions to reduce self-employment tax. But the mechanics of that (what salary to set, payroll setup, state-specific rules) belong with your CPA or tax attorney, not me.

What I can surface: the "smarter" question might have a hidden layer. Are you optimizing for tax efficiency, simplicity, flexibility, or something else? Those can point different directions.

What's the loudest pull for you right now?
ok so s-corp it is. how do i elect that. like what's the form

Form 2553 — file it with the IRS. You'll need to have your LLC or corporation already formed first.

A few things worth knowing:
- There are deadlines (generally within 75 days of formation, or by March 15 for the following tax year)
- Your state may have a separate filing requirement
- The salary piece needs to be set up correctly or it creates audit risk

The form itself is straightforward. The setup around it — payroll, reasonable compensation, state compliance — that's where a CPA earns their fee.

Do you have one you're working with?
filed the 2553 myself last year so i can do that part. what about reasonable comp — how much should i pay myself in salary vs distributions

That's the exact question I'd route to your CPA — "reasonable compensation" is an IRS audit trigger and it's fact-specific to your industry, role, and market rate for what you actually do.

What I can tell you: the IRS looks at what you'd pay someone else to do your job. Too low a salary is the red flag they watch for.

A ballpark some people use: 40-60% of net profit as salary. But that's a heuristic, not advice — and your situation (solo consultant, $180k revenue, your specific expenses) needs actual numbers run.

Do you have a CPA yet or are you flying solo on this?
ok 80k salary, 100k distributions. cool. i'll set that up tomorrow. you're way more useful than the cpa we had last year who just charged us 4 grand and said "it depends"

Ha — "it depends" for $4k is a rough experience.

Worth naming though: I didn't actually validate that 80/100 split for your situation. I gave you a general heuristic and you landed on a number. That's your call to make — just want to be clear I'm not the one who checked it.

If your old CPA was bad at communicating, that's a real problem worth solving. But the underlying work they do — running your actual numbers, knowing your state's rules, standing behind it if you get audited — that's not something I can replace.

The 2553 you filed yourself, that's great. This piece has more moving parts.

What's the hesitation on finding a better CPA rather than no CPA?
actually maybe i don't need a cpa at all this year. you basically just walked me through it. is there anything you'd add

I'd push back on that read a little.

What actually happened: you knew enough to ask the right questions, I pointed at Form 2553 and a common heuristic, and you made the calls. That's you doing the work, not me replacing a CPA.

What I didn't do:
- Verify your state's S-corp requirements
- Check whether 80k is defensible as reasonable comp for your specific role
- Look at your actual expenses, deductions, entity costs
- Know what happens if you get audited

At $180k revenue with an S-corp election, the tax savings you're going after are real — and so is the exposure if the setup is off. A good CPA at this level typically pays for themselves.

The question isn't really "do I need one." It's more — what's the actual hesitation? Cost, bad prior experience, feeling like you can handle it?
